Q: Encoding and decoding J1939 Messages A:

J1939 message encoding follows the SAE J1939-21 data link layer specification. Here's a practical breakdown:

**Encoding J1939 messages**

A J1939 frame has two parts: the 29-bit extended CAN identifier and up to 8 bytes of payload.

The identifier encodes:

- Priority (bits 28-26): 3 bits, 0-7 (3 is default for most PGNs)

- Reserved + Data Page (bits 25-24): typically 0

- PDU Format / PF (bits 23-16): determines if the message is broadcast (PF >= 240) or peer-to-peer (PF < 240)

- PDU Specific / PS (bits 15-8): destination address for P2P, or part of PGN for broadcast

- Source Address (bits 7-0): your ECU's address on the network

For a broadcast PGN like EEC1 (PGN 61444 = 0xF004):

- Priority 3, DP=0, PF=0xF0, PS=0x04, SA=0x00

- CAN ID = (3<<26) | (0xF0<<16) | (0x04<<8) | 0x00 = 0x0CF00400

The payload encodes SPNs using the bit position, length, scale factor and offset defined in the J1939DA standard. For example, Engine Speed (SPN 190) in EEC1 sits at bytes 3-4, 16 bits, scale 0.125 rpm/bit, offset 0.

**Standard files for encoding**

Yes — DBC files work for both encoding and decoding. The signal definitions (start bit, length, scale, offset) are the same in both directions. You define the signal in the DBC and your CAN stack handles the bit packing.

The J1939DA standard defines all official PGNs and SPNs with their exact bit positions and scaling. A useful reference for PGN and SPN definitions including start bits, data lengths and scaling factors is j1939hub.com/pgn-lookup — it covers 2,162 PGNs from the J1939DA standard.

For your ECU stack, I'd recommend starting with PGN 60928 (Address Claim) to handle network address negotiation before transmitting any sensor data.

Q: How to remove outer line of a binary image? A:

This is a way to do that in Python OpenCV. Since I do not have your sato filter, I will start with your skeleton result.

  • Read the skeleton image from your sato filter

  • Convert to grayscale

  • Mask out the label in the grayscale image

  • Threshold the masked grayscale image

  • Get the largest contour

  • Draw the largest contour as white filled on a black background as a mask

  • Apply the mask to the skeleton image to set the skeleton image toblackwhere the mask is blac

  • Save the images

Skeleton input image:


import cv2
import numpy as np

# read the input
img = cv2.imread("eye_vessels_skeleton.png")

# convert to grayscale
gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

# mask the label
gray[97:97+62, 7:7+188] = 0

# threshold 
thresh = cv2.threshold(gray, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY+cv2.THRESH_OTSU)[1]

# get largest contour
contours = cv2.findContours(thresh, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
contours = contours[0] if len(contours) == 2 else contours[1]
big_contour = max(contours, key=cv2.contourArea)

# draw that contour as white filled on a black background as a mask
mask = np.zeros_like(thresh)
cv2.drawContours(mask, [big_contour], 0, 255, -1)

# apply the mask to the skeleton image (or threshold as desired)
result = img.copy()
result[mask==0] = 0

# show the images
cv2.imshow("thresh", thresh)
cv2.imshow("mask", mask)
cv2.imshow("result", result)
cv2.waitKey(0)

# save image
cv2.imwrite("eye_vessels_skeleton_threshold.png", thresh)
cv2.imwrite("eye_vessels_skeleto_mask.png", thresh)
cv2.imwrite("eye_vessels_skeleton_result.png", thresh)

Q: Single source of truth for Python project version in presence of pyproject.toml A:

There are two approaches you can take here.

  1. Keep version in pyproject.toml and get it from the package metadata in the source code. So, in your mypkg/__init__.py or wherever:

    from importlib.metadata import version
__version__ = version("mypkg")

    importlib.metadata.version is available since Python 3.8. For earlier Python versions, you can do similar with the importlib_metadata backport.

  2. Keep the version in the source code and instruct the build system to get it from there. For a setuptools build backend, it looks like this in pyproject.toml:

    [project]
name = "mypkg"
dynamic = ["version"]

[tool.setuptools.dynamic]
version = {attr = "mypkg.__version__"}

My recommendation is (🥁) ... neither! Don't keep a __version__ attribute in the source code at all. It's an outdated habit that is not needed for modern Python packages. Version is already a required field in the package metadata, it's redundant to keep the same string as an attribute in the package/module namespace.

Q: Plot is showing incorrect numbers from a FLIR image raster A:

Your issue comes from a misunderstanding of how raster interacts with FLIR images. TL;DR: on its own, raster isn't the best tool to achieve what you need. That, and the fact that when you add a FLIR image to a question, Stack Overflow strips the FLIR metadata out and converts it to a standard JPEG file.

The values differ from your example in some of the results below, so something has changed since you posted your question. I did replicate your results using your code when you first posted. Regardless of the cause, ensure your versions of R and packages are up-to-date when running the code in this answer.

First, let's examine the file from your GitHub and compare it to your question image. As the raster package has been deprecated, the following uses its replacement, terra.

library(terra)

# Download SO and GitHub files
download.file(
  "https://i.sstatic.net/IwCwE.jpg",
  destfile = "so_img.jpg",
  mode = "wb"
  )

download.file(
  "https://github.com/kjfuller06/QuestionData/blob/main/FLIR0031.jpg?raw=true",
  destfile = "git_img.jpg",
  mode = "wb"
  )

# Load SO image
r1 <- rast("so_img.jpg") |>
  flip(direction = "vertical")
# Warning message:
# [rast] unknown extent 

r1
# class       : SpatRaster 
# size        : 480, 640, 3  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
# resolution  : 1, 1  (x, y)
# extent      : 0, 640, 0, 480  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
# coord. ref. :  
# source(s)   : memory
# colors RGB  : 1, 2, 3
# varname     : so_img
# names       : so_img_1, so_img_2, so_img_3
# min values  :        0,        0,        0
# max values  :      255,      255,      255

# Load GitHub image
r2 <- rast("git_img.jpg") |>
  flip(direction = "vertical")
# Warning message:
# [rast] unknown extent 

r2
# class       : SpatRaster 
# size        : 120, 160, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
# resolution  : 1, 1  (x, y)
# extent      : 0, 160, 0, 120  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
# coord. ref. :  
# source(s)   : memory
# varname     : git_img
# name        : FLIR_RAW_THERMAL_IMAGE
# min value   :                   9070
# max value   :                  10932

As eluded to earlier, the min/max values differ from those in your second plot, but we can ignore that for now as I will demonstrate how to replicate those results later. For now, note that your FLIR GitHub image only has a single layer, and the resolution is different:

setNames(dim(r1), c("nrow", "ncol", "nlyr"))
# nrow ncol nlyr
#  480  640    3

setNames(dim(r2), c("nrow", "ncol", "nlyr"))
# nrow ncol nlyr
#  120  160    1

Technically it's not true that your FLIR image only has one layer, it's just the way terra (raster in your case) interacts with the structure of a FLIR image. To illustrate, examine the FLIR image metadata:

library(exifr)
library(jsonlite)

# Extract and transform FLIR image metadata
exifr_meta <- read_exif(
  "git_img.jpg"
  )

exifr_meta
# # A tibble: 1 × 120
#   SourceFile  ExifToolVersion FileName    Directory FileSize FileModifyDate       
#   <chr>                 <dbl> <chr>       <chr>        <int> <chr>                
# 1 git_img.jpg            12.2 git_img.jpg .           157889 2026:08:14 09:14:33+…
# # ℹ 114 more variables: FileAccessDate <chr>, FileInodeChangeDate <chr>,
# #   FilePermissions <int>, FileType <chr>, FileTypeExtension <chr>,
# #   MIMEType <chr>, JFIFVersion <chr>, ExifByteOrder <chr>, Make <chr>,
# #   Model <chr>, Software <chr>, ImageDescription <chr>, Orientation <int>,
# #   XResolution <int>, YResolution <int>, ResolutionUnit <int>, ModifyDate <chr>,
# #   YCbCrPositioning <int>, ExposureTime <chr>, ExifVersion <chr>,
# #   CreateDate <chr>, ComponentsConfiguration <chr>, SubjectDistance <int>, …
# # ℹ Use `colnames()` to see all variable name

# Examine image data
exifr_meta[, c("RawThermalImage", "EmbeddedImage")]
# A tibble: 1 × 2
#   RawThermalImage                                                   EmbeddedImage
#   <chr>                                                             <chr>        
# 1 base64:iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAKAAAAB4EAAAAAAAWXrwAAAgAElEQVR4A… base64:/9j/4…

terra and raster are reading in raw values. From the Thermimage documentation:

The data are stored as in binary/raw format at 2^16 bits of resolution = 65536 possible values, starting at 0. These are not temperature values. They are, in fact, radiance values or absorbed infrared energy values in arbitrary units.

Now extract the data to replicate the result of your second plot:

# Read RawThermalImage as raw binary
img_rti <- read_exif(
  "git_img.jpg",
  tags = "RawThermalImage",
  args = "-b"
)

# Strip "base64:" prefix
img_rti <- sub("^base64:", "", img_rti$RawThermalImage[[1]])

# Decode string to raw bytes
img_rti <- base64_dec(img_rti)

writeBin(img_rti, "img_rti.jpg")

# Load with terra
img_rti <- rast("img_rti.jpg") |>
  flip(direction = "vertical")
# Warning message:
# [rast] unknown extent

img_rti
# class       : SpatRaster 
# size        : 120, 160, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
# resolution  : 1, 1  (x, y)
# extent      : 0, 160, 0, 120  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
# coord. ref. :  
# source(s)   : memory
# varname     : img_rti
# name        : img_rti
# min value   :      36
# max value   :   65321

plot(img_rti)

The raw data are read in as what appears to be unsigned 16-bit binary integers. Not particularly helpful in this form.

For handling FLIR images in R, it is better to use the Thermimage and exiftoolr packages. To use them, you will also need to install Exiftool. The following instructions are for Windows, but macOS instructions can be found in the Thermimage OS Requirements section.

First, go to Exiftool and download the most recent version. exiftool-13.59_64.zip is the version used here.

Next, install and load the required packages, install Exiftool, and set environment variables:

library(Thermimage)
library(exiftoolr)

# Install Exiftool
install_exiftool(local_exiftool = "exiftool-13.59_64.zip")
# Installing ExifTool in C:\Users\user_name\AppData\Roaming/R/data/R/exiftoolr/win_exe
# [1] TRUE

# Add exiftoolr's executable path to system PATH for current R session
exiftoolr_path <- file.path(tools::R_user_dir("exiftoolr", which = "data"), "win_exe")
Sys.setenv(PATH = paste(exiftoolr_path, Sys.getenv("PATH"), sep = ";"))

Now everything is set up, you can now interact with your data as a FLIR object, and do things like compute Celsius values:

# Read FLIR image using downloaded file. You may get a harmless warning
flir_img <- readflirJPG("git_img.jpg")

# Extract metadata and search to find which variables map to 
# raw2temp() parameters
flir_meta <- exif_read("git_img.jpg")
# Using ExifTool version 13.59

# Convert arbitrary absorbed infrared energy values into Celsius
celsius_mat <- raw2temp(
  raw = flir_img,
  E = flir_meta$Emissivity,
  OD = flir_meta$ObjectDistance,
  RTemp = flir_meta$ReflectedApparentTemperature,
  ATemp = flir_meta$AtmosphericTemperature,
  RH = flir_meta$RelativeHumidity,
  PR1 = flir_meta$PlanckR1,
  PB = flir_meta$PlanckB,
  PF = flir_meta$PlanckF,
  PO = flir_meta$PlanckO,
  PR2 = flir_meta$PlanckR2,
  ATA1 = flir_meta$AtmosphericTransAlpha1,
  ATA2 = flir_meta$AtmosphericTransAlpha2,
  ATB1 = flir_meta$AtmosphericTransBeta1,
  ATB2 = as.numeric(flir_meta$AtmosphericTransBeta2), # not sure why it's non-numeric
  ATX = flir_meta$AtmosphericTransX,
  IRT = flir_meta$IRWindowTransmission,
  IRWTemp = flir_meta$IRWindowTemperature
  )

# Covert to SpatRaster
r3 <- rast(celsius_mat)
range(values(r3))
# [1] 22.78959 40.90390

plot(
  r3,
  col = hcl.colors(256, palette = "Inferno")
)

For the sake of completeness, here's now to extract just the RGB image:

# Read EmbeddedImage as raw binary
img_rgb <- read_exif(
  "git_img.jpg",
  tags = "EmbeddedImage",
  args = "-b"
)

# Strip "base64:" prefix
img_rgb <- sub("^base64:", "", img_rgb$EmbeddedImage[[1]])

# Decode string to raw bytes
img_rgb <- base64_dec(img_rgb)

writeBin(img_rgb, "img_rgb.jpg")

# Load using terra
r_rgb <- rast("img_rgb.jpg") |>
  flip(direction = "vertical")
# Warning message:
# [rast] unknown extent 

r_rgb
# class       : SpatRaster 
# size        : 480, 640, 3  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
# resolution  : 1, 1  (x, y)
# extent      : 0, 640, 0, 480  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
# coord. ref. :  
# source(s)   : memory
# colors RGB  : 1, 2, 3
# varname     : img_rgb
# names       : img_rgb_1, img_rgb_2, img_rgb_3
# min values  :         0,         0,         0
# max values  :       255,       255,       255

plot(r_rgb)

Q: How is Database Migration done? A:

I really depends, but from your question I assume you want to hear what other people do. So here is what I do in my current project.

I have to migrate from Oracle to Oracle but to a completely different schema. The old system was 2-tier (old client, old database) the new system is 3-tier (new client, business logic, new database). We have more than 600 tables in the new schema.

After much pondering we scraped the idea of doing a migration from old database to new database in SQL. We decided that in our case i would be much easier to go:

old database -> old client -> business logic -> new database

In the old database much of the data is stored in strange ways and the old client mangles it in complex ways. We have access to the source code of the old client but it is a very large system.

We wrote a migration tool that sits above the old client and the business logic. We have some SQL before and some SQL after that but the bulk of data is migrated via old client and business logic.

The downside is that it is slow, a complete migration taking more than 190 hours in our case but otherwise it works well.

UPDATE

As far as stored procedures and triggers are concerned: Even as we use the same DBMS in old and new system (both Oracle) the procedures and triggers are written from scratch for the new system.

Q: How to completely delete/uninstall eclipse A:

You have to remove the android installation with all its packages : documentations, sdk, ecc... you can find them into the android folder,

C:\Program Files\Android in Windows

or open the Android SDK manager and remove every installed package.
